title: The structure of the field equations
one_line_summary: Before any solution is attempted, the chapter examines what kind of equations G_ab = 8 pi T_ab are: how they can be read, why they are under-determined by exactly the coordinate freedom, why non-linearity makes them hard, how the cosmological term fits, how conservation implies geodesic motion, how the vacuum equations split into six evolution equations and four constraints that propagate via the Bianchi identities (analytic Cauchy-Kowalevskaya route, then smooth harmonic-gauge route), and what the hole problem, the equivalence problem and the catalogue of exact solutions teach about solutions as geometries rather than coordinate expressions.
role_in_book: Chapters 9-12 motivated and derived the field equations (principles, geodesic deviation, variational principle, energy-momentum tensors). Chapter 13 is the pause between derivation and solution: it establishes the mathematical character of the equations (well-posedness, gauge freedom, constraints, non-linearity, conservation, equivalence of metrics) so that Chapter 14 can recast the Cauchy problem geometrically in the 3+1 and 2+2 formalisms, and Chapters 15 onward can build exact solutions (Schwarzschild, black holes, gravitational waves, cosmology) with a clear sense of what an exact solution is worth. It also sets up recurring themes: Lambda for cosmology (Chapters 24-26), linearization (Chapter 21), and numerical relativity (Chapter 14).

learning_objectives: Reader can state three ways to read G_ab = 8 pi T_ab (geometry from matter, matter from geometry, simultaneous constraints) and say why the second route usually yields unphysical matter.
Reader can count equations versus unknowns for the vacuum equations and explain how the four contracted Bianchi identities and the four-function coordinate freedom balance each other.
Reader can explain why the field equations are non-linear, why superposition fails, and how gravitational self-coupling expresses the non-linearity physically.
Reader can state the Lichnerowicz junction conditions for a metric across a surface of discontinuity.
Reader can write the field equations with a cosmological term, show that the term is compatible with conservation, and recount why Einstein introduced and later abandoned it.
Reader can show that nabla_b T^ab = 0 applied to dust forces geodesic motion of the dust worldlines.
Reader can explain the Cauchy problem for the wave equation by generating a Taylor series from initial data and can state the Cauchy-Kowalevskaya theorem.

Reader can split R_ab = 0 into R_00, R_0alpha, R_alphabeta equations, identify which second time derivatives appear, and name the under-determination (gauge) and over-determination (constraints) problems.
Reader can show that when R_alphabeta = 0 the remaining equations are equivalent to G_a^0 = 0 and argue from the contracted Bianchi identity that constraints satisfied initially remain satisfied.
Reader can define harmonic coordinates, write the harmonic gauge condition, and explain why the reduced Einstein equations are a hyperbolic system solvable for smooth data (Choquet-Bruhat).
Reader can explain the hole argument and why a spacetime is an equivalence class of (manifold, metric) pairs related by diffeomorphisms.
Reader can describe the equivalence problem and outline the Cartan-Karlhede approach to deciding whether two metrics are the same geometry.
Reader can assess the status of exact solutions: how they are found (symmetry, ansatz), why computer algebra matters, and which physically important problems lack exact solutions.

teaching_approach.summary: A survey-style chapter that steps back from the derived field equations and interrogates them as a system of PDEs. It alternates short conceptual discussions (interpretations, non-linearity, Lambda, hole problem, exact solutions) with one sustained mathematical argument (the Cauchy problem), which is built by first rehearsing the Taylor-series method on the flat wave equation, then applying it component by component to R_ab = 0, then replacing analyticity by harmonic gauge. Counting arguments (10 equations, 4 identities, 4 coordinate functions) organize the whole chapter, and computer algebra anecdotes from the authors' own research ground the claims about complexity.
narrative_arc: Ask how the field equations should be read: three directions of inference between g_ab and T_ab.
Count equations and unknowns; recognise Bianchi identities and coordinate freedom as matching fourfold redundancies; introduce gauge conditions.
Explain non-linearity physically (field energy gravitates) and preview the three escape routes: symmetry, approximation, numerics.
Set differentiability and junction conditions aside with a smoothness assumption.
Add the cosmological term, check it respects conservation, recount Einstein's Machian motive and the reversal after the discovery of expansion and de Sitter's solution.
Show that the field equations already contain the equations of motion: conservation plus dust gives geodesics.
Pose the Cauchy problem; rehearse it on the wave equation with analytic data; state Cauchy-Kowalevskaya.
Apply the rehearsal to vacuum GR: split R_ab, locate the second time derivatives, discover gauge freedom in g_0a and constraints R_00, R_0alpha.
Prove that constraints propagate by the contracted Bianchi identity, yielding the Lichnerowicz normal form.
Criticise analyticity on causal grounds and upgrade to smooth data using harmonic coordinates and the reduced (hyperbolic) Einstein equations; mention the global maximal development theorem.
Confront the hole problem to clarify that solutions are geometries, not coordinate expressions.
Ask how to tell two metrics apart: the equivalence problem, Cartan and Karlhede, computer algebra.
Close with a sober appraisal of exact solutions: many found, few physical, key problems unsolved, hence approximation and numerical relativity.
signature_moves: Rehearse a hard existence argument on a trivial model first: the flat wave equation is solved by repeated differentiation and Taylor series before the same machinery is turned on R_ab = 0.
Organise the analysis around explicit counting (10 equations, 4 Bianchi identities, 4 coordinate functions, 6 evolution equations, 4 constraints).
Diagnose problems by locating second time derivatives: only g_alphabeta,00 appear, and only in specific combinations, which exposes both gauge freedom and constraints at once.
Use the Leibniz-rule-plus-normalisation trick on dust to make the abstract claim that field equations imply geodesic motion concrete in four lines.

Tie abstract issues to Einstein's personal history: the cosmological 'blunder' and the eight years of hole-argument confusion.

Repeatedly identify the same principle from different angles: solutions are equivalence classes under coordinate transformation (determinacy in §13.2, gauge in §13.6, hole problem in §13.8, equivalence problem in §13.9).

sections.title: Interpretation of the field equations
sections.summary: Offers three readings of G_ab = 8 pi T_ab. Read right to left, it determines geometry from a prescribed matter distribution, a Machian stance that falls short because matter alone does not fix a unique geometry; vacuum is the central case. Read left to right, one could invent any metric and compute the matter it needs, but this almost always gives matter with negative energy density or other violations of the dominant energy condition. Read as ten relations among twenty quantities, the equations constrain g_ab and T_ab jointly, as in the Einstein-Maxwell system where the Maxwell field and metric are solved together.
key_moves: Direction of inference as an organising question.
Reject 'metric first, read off T' because generic choices give negative energy density.
Coupled-system view illustrated by Einstein-Maxwell (12.57), (12.58).

sections.title: Determinacy, non-linearity, and differentiability
sections.summary: Ten vacuum equations for ten metric components look well posed, but the contracted Bianchi identities impose four differential relations among them, so there are effectively fewer equations than unknowns. This is exactly compensated by the freedom to change coordinates with four arbitrary functions, so solutions are equivalence classes and one may impose four gauge conditions, for example Gaussian normal coordinates. The equations are non-linear, which kills superposition; physically the gravitational field carries energy and hence mass that itself gravitates. Einstein doubted exact solutions would ever be found, but Schwarzschild found one in 1916 by imposing spherical symmetry; thousands are now known, mostly via symmetry. Otherwise one uses approximations (weak fields, far from sources, linearised theory) or numerical relativity based on the 3+1 formalism. Fields are assumed smooth; the minimal requirement is a C^2 metric, and across surfaces such as a star's boundary the Lichnerowicz conditions require continuity of g_ab and its first derivatives only.
key_moves: 10 equations minus 4 identities versus 10 unknowns minus 4 coordinate functions.
Solutions as equivalence classes; gauge fixing picks a representative.
Self-coupling argument: field energy is mass is source.
Three routes past non-linearity: symmetry, approximation, numerics.
Smoothness assumption and junction conditions.

sections.title: The cosmological term
sections.summary: Einstein disliked that the vacuum equations admit Minkowski space, which contradicts the Machian form M2 (no matter, no geometry); a lone test body in such a universe would still have inertia. Asymptotic flatness as a boundary condition does not exclude flat space. Seeking a static, homogeneous, closed universe to supply boundary conditions, he added Lambda g_ab, which is compatible with conservation because the metric is covariantly constant, and corresponds to adding 2 Lambda to R in the Lagrangian. Generally covariant, second-order equations linear in T_ab must equate kappa T_ab to a combination of the Ricci tensor, the Ricci scalar times the metric (coefficient mu) and a constant times the metric, and conservation fixes mu = -1/2; Hilbert found the equations variationally the same year. Lambda removes flat space as a solution, but the discovery of cosmic expansion, expanding closed models without Lambda, and de Sitter's Lambda-vacuum solution led Einstein to renounce it. There is nevertheless no reason to omit it; it is negligible locally, may be moved to the right-hand side as dark energy, and in Newtonian cosmology Lambda > 0 gives universal repulsion.

Static closed cosmology forces an extra term.
nabla g = 0 makes Lambda g_ab compatible with nabla T = 0.
General form (13.8); conservation fixes mu.
Historical reversal: expansion, Friedmann-type models, de Sitter vacuum.
Reinterpret Lambda as a source (dark energy).

sections.title: The conservation equations
sections.summary: The geodesic postulates of the axiomatic formulation need not be assumed separately in general relativity: because test matter is itself part of T_ab and the Bianchi identities force nabla_b T^ab = 0, the equations of motion are contained in the field equations. The historical proofs (Einstein-Grommer, Einstein-Infeld-Hoffmann) treated particles as field singularities and were very involved; later work by Geroch-Jang and Gralla-Wald confirmed them. A short dust calculation illustrates the mechanism: expand the divergence of rho_0 u^a u^b with the Leibniz rule, contract with u_a using the normalisation of u to get conservation of rest mass flux, and substitute back to obtain the geodesic equation.
concepts: equations of motion from the field equations

Split rho_0 u^a u^b as (rho_0 u^b) times u^a.
Contract with u_a; u_a nabla_b u^a = 0 from normalisation.
Continuity equation nabla_b(rho_0 u^b) = 0.
Back-substitute to get u^b nabla_b u^a = 0.

sections.title: The Cauchy problem
sections.summary: States the initial value problem: from the metric and its first derivatives on a spacelike hypersurface, construct the future spacetime. Since spatial derivatives follow from g_ab on the slice, the data reduce to g_ab and g_ab,0. If the field equations yield g_ab,00, repeated time differentiation gives all higher derivatives, and for analytic metrics a Taylor series in x^0 along coordinate lines reconstructs the metric. The method is rehearsed on the flat wave equation: phi and phi_t on t = 0 determine every time derivative through the equation and its t-derivatives, and analyticity of the data bounds the series. The Cauchy-Kowalevskaya theorem generalises this to analytic second-order systems solved for the second time derivatives, with proof by majorization.
key_moves: Initial data reduce to g_ab and g_ab,0 on Sigma_0.
Goal: solve for g_ab,00, then differentiate repeatedly.
Taylor expansion (13.11) along an x^0 curve.
Wave-equation rehearsal (13.12)-(13.15).
Theorem (13.16)-(13.17) with proof idea: majorizing series and uniqueness from zero data.

sections.title: Einstein's equations as evolution equations
sections.summary: With x^0 timelike, the vacuum equations split into R_00, R_0alpha and R_alphabeta parts. Each contains second time derivatives only of the spatial metric g_alphabeta, plus terms fixed by the initial data. Two problems follow: g_0a,00 never appears (under-determination, which is the gauge freedom, handled by prescribing g_0a, e.g. Gaussian normal coordinates or a choice of lapse and shift), and ten equations constrain six unknowns (over-determination, meaning the data must satisfy constraints). R_alphabeta = 0 are the evolution equations solvable by Cauchy-Kowalevskaya. Given R_alphabeta = 0, R_00 and R_0alpha are equivalent to G_a^0 = 0, and all other Einstein components can be written in terms of G_a^0, giving Lichnerowicz's normal form. The contracted Bianchi identity then gives a linear homogeneous first-order system for G_a^0, so zero initial values propagate. For analytic data and gauge the vacuum Cauchy problem is thus solved uniquely in the chosen coordinates. Analyticity clashes with causality, motivating Choquet-Bruhat's 1952 smooth-data theorem.
key_moves: Locate second time derivatives in (13.21)-(13.23).
Prescribe g_0a as a gauge choice.
Solve R_alphabeta = 0 as evolution equations.

Bianchi identity (13.31) gives homogeneous linear evolution of G_a^0; zero solution by uniqueness.
Analytic functions are determined everywhere by a neighbourhood, incompatible with finite signal speed.

sections.title: Solving Einstein's equations in harmonic coordinates
sections.summary: Harmonic coordinates are those whose coordinate functions obey the curved wave equation, equivalently g^cd Gamma^a_cd = 0. In any coordinates the Ricci tensor equals a reduced part, whose principal term is -1/2 g^cd g_ab,cd, plus symmetrised derivatives of H_a. In harmonic gauge the vacuum equations become the reduced Einstein equations, a quasi-linear hyperbolic system for all ten metric components, solvable for smooth data by standard theory. To make a reduced solution a true solution, choose data with g_00 = 1, g_0alpha = 0 satisfying the constraints for the spatial metric and its time derivative, then pick g_0b,0 so H_a vanishes initially; the constraints make H_a,0 vanish too, and the Bianchi identity gives a wave equation for H_a, so H_a stays zero. The global result of Choquet-Bruhat and Geroch gives a unique maximal development containing every solution with the same data; stability and extendibility are active research.
key_moves: Box x^a = 0 is equivalent to H^a = 0.
Decompose R_ab = R^H_ab + H_(a,b).
Reduced equations are wave equations for g_ab.
Choose initial g_0b,0 so H_a = 0 on Sigma_0; constraints give H_a,0 = 0.
Bianchi identity makes H_a obey a wave equation; uniqueness keeps H_a = 0.
