sections.title: The hole problem
sections.summary: Revisits the Cauchy problem's hidden assumption of a bare manifold. Einstein's hole argument: if matter is fixed outside a region H, the field equations fix the metric inside, yet a transformation that is the identity outside H but drags points inside H produces a second, functionally different metric, apparently contradicting determinism. The resolution is that points of a bare manifold carry no physical identity until a metric is present; the two metrics describe the same physical spacetime. A spacetime is a manifold with a metric, and physically equivalent spacetimes form an equivalence class under coordinate transformations. The issue contributed to the eight-year delay between Einstein's first general covariance ideas and the final equations.
key_moves: Fix matter outside H; move points inside only.
Compare functional forms of g and g-bar.
Argue that points acquire identity only through the metric.
Define physical solutions as equivalence classes.

sections.title: The equivalence problem
sections.summary: Given two metrics, how does one decide whether a coordinate transformation relates them? Cartan's classical solution compares the Riemann tensors and their covariant derivatives up to tenth order, far beyond what computer algebra (Mathematica, Maple, Reduce, and the relativity-specific SHEEP with CLASSI and STENSOR) can do. Karlhede's 1980 algorithm fixes a canonical tetrad stage by stage so the Riemann tensor and its derivatives take standard form, producing invariants; the theoretical worst case needs seven derivatives, five for vacuum (Ramos and Vickers 1996), and in practice three or fewer. If the invariant sets differ, the metrics differ; if they agree, one solves four algebraic equations for the transformation.
key_moves: Pose equivalence as existence of a coordinate transformation.
Cartan: compare Riemann and derivatives to 10th order.
Karlhede: canonical frames reduce the order needed.
Decision procedure: compare invariants, then solve algebraic equations.

sections.title: The status of exact solutions
sections.summary: Written out in full, the Ricci tensor for a general metric has of order 100,000 terms; d'Inverno's LAM program first produced this output, a sample of which is reproduced. Despite Einstein's pessimism, Schwarzschild found the static spherically symmetric vacuum solution a month or so after publication, and the vacuum equations in fact force spherical symmetry to imply staticity. It generalises to Kerr-Newman, which isolated black holes approach. Ansatz methods such as Harrison's separation of variables yielded forty vacuum metrics, checked with LAM, and classified with SHEEP and CLASSI, which revealed two to be the same. Schwarzschild's solution has been rediscovered about twenty times. Kramer et al. catalogue known solutions. Many are unphysical, and no exact solutions exist for the two-body problem, the interiors of black holes, or radiation from an isolated source, so approximation methods and numerical relativity are required.
key_moves: Quantify complexity: ~10^5 terms in R_ab.
Symmetry assumptions made the first solution possible.
Non-linear PDEs can force extra structure (spherical implies static).
Invariant classification exposes duplicate solutions.
Weigh physical relevance; list unsolved problems.

sections.title: Exercises and further reading
sections.summary: Thirteen exercises on the Lambda Lagrangian and uniqueness, trace-free Einstein-Maxwell alternative, perfect fluid conservation and vorticity, the component forms of the Cauchy analysis, harmonic gauge, and a reflective computer-algebra exercise. Further reading points to Adler-Bazin-Schiffer and Wald for the Cauchy problem, Ringstrom for a full treatment, d'Inverno (1980) for algebraic computing and Kramer et al. for exact solutions.
key_moves: Exercises fill in the component calculations deferred in §13.5-13.7.

concepts.name: Einstein field equations
concepts.definition: The ten second-order partial differential equations G_ab = 8 pi T_ab (relativistic units) relating the Einstein tensor of the spacetime metric to the energy-momentum tensor of matter and non-gravitational fields.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapters 10-12 and interrogated as a PDE system: which way to read it, how many independent equations it contains, and what type of problem it poses.

concepts.name: three readings of the field equations
concepts.definition: The field equations can be used to find the metric from given matter (right to left), to find the matter required by a chosen metric (left to right), or as joint constraints on metric and matter solved simultaneously.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening framing of the chapter, with a verdict on each: the Machian first reading is incomplete, the second gives unphysical matter, the third is standard for coupled systems like Einstein-Maxwell.

concepts.name: vacuum solution
concepts.definition: A metric satisfying G_ab = 0, equivalently R_ab = 0 in four dimensions, describing regions with no matter or non-gravitational fields.
concepts.how_introduced: Singled out as the most important case of reading the equations right to left, then used throughout the Cauchy analysis for simplicity.

concepts.name: dominant energy condition
concepts.definition: The requirement that every timelike observer measures non-negative energy density and a causal (non-spacelike) energy flux; used as a test of whether a T_ab is physically reasonable.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to explain why inventing a metric and reading off T_ab is rarely useful: the resulting matter typically has negative energy density somewhere.

concepts.name: Einstein-Maxwell equations
concepts.definition: The coupled system of Einstein's equations sourced by the Maxwell energy-momentum tensor together with Maxwell's equations F^ab_;b = 0 on the curved background, F_ab = phi_a,b - phi_b,a.
concepts.how_introduced: Example of the third reading, where metric and field are determined jointly.

concepts.name: contracted Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: The identities nabla_b G^ab = 0 satisfied by the Einstein tensor of any metric, giving four differential relations among its ten components.
concepts.how_introduced: First as the reason the ten vacuum equations are not independent, then as the source of conservation laws and equations of motion, then as the engine that propagates the constraints and the harmonic gauge condition.

concepts.name: under-determinacy of the field equations
concepts.definition: Because of four identities, the ten field equations do not fix all ten metric components; the undetermined fourfold freedom corresponds exactly to coordinate transformations, so the metric is determined only up to diffeomorphism.
concepts.how_introduced: Counting argument in §13.2; reappears in §13.6 as the absence of g_0a,00 from the split equations.

concepts.name: gauge condition
concepts.definition: Four conditions imposed on the metric components (or connection) that use up the freedom to choose coordinates, selecting a representative of the equivalence class of metrics describing the same geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the natural response to under-determinacy, with Gaussian normal coordinates as the first example and harmonic coordinates later.

concepts.name: Gaussian normal coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates built by labelling points of a spacelike hypersurface with spatial coordinates, carrying these labels along geodesics that leave the surface orthogonally, and using proper time (affine parameter) along the geodesics as x^0, so that g_00 = 1 and g_0alpha = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Quick example of a gauge in §13.2; constructed geometrically in §13.6 as a concrete way to prescribe g_0a.

concepts.name: non-linearity of the field equations
concepts.definition: The field equations are non-linear in the metric and its derivatives, so the sum of two solutions is generally not a solution; physically, gravitational field energy acts as a source of gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the main source of difficulty, explained via mass-energy equivalence, and used to justify symmetry, approximation and numerical methods.

concepts.name: linearized field equations
concepts.definition: Approximation in which the metric is a small perturbation of flat spacetime and only terms linear in the perturbation are kept in the field equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed as the approximation route when gravity is weak, e.g. far from an isolated source.

concepts.name: numerical relativity
concepts.definition: Solving Einstein's equations approximately on a computer, typically by evolving initial data forward in time using a 3+1 split of spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed in §13.2 (binary black hole waveforms for gravitational-wave detection) and invoked in §13.10 as the necessary recourse where exact solutions are missing.

concepts.name: Lichnerowicz junction conditions
concepts.definition: Across a hypersurface of discontinuity such as the surface of a body, the metric and its first derivatives must be continuous, while second and higher derivatives may jump.
concepts.how_introduced: Brief remark on differentiability, likened to the continuity conditions of Newtonian potential theory, after assuming C-infinity fields (C^2 being enough to define G_ab).
concepts.notes: Stated in a particular coordinate system; the coordinate-invariant Israel-Darmois conditions are not mentioned.

concepts.name: cosmological constant
concepts.definition: A constant Lambda multiplying the metric in a term added to the field equations, G_ab - Lambda g_ab = 8 pi T_ab in this book's signature; positive Lambda acts as a universal repulsion and is equivalent to a constant vacuum energy source.
concepts.how_introduced: Through Einstein's attempt to build a static, homogeneous, closed universe that would supply Machian boundary conditions, followed by the history of its rejection and the modern dark-energy reinterpretation.

concepts.name: Mach's principle
concepts.definition: The idea that matter determines inertia and geometry. The book's form M2 (set out in §9.2) says that where there is no matter there should be no geometry, so a vacuum solution such as Minkowski space violates it; the related form M3 says that a lone body in an otherwise empty universe should have no inertial properties.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain Einstein's dissatisfaction with vacuum equations admitting Minkowski space and his motive for the cosmological term; also used to label the right-to-left reading of the equations as Machian.
concepts.notes: Forms M1-M3 were set out in DIV §9.2: M1 matter fixes geometry, M2 no matter means no geometry, M3 no inertia for a body alone in an empty universe. §13.3 cites M2 and illustrates it with the inertia of a lone test body.

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: A boundary condition requiring the Riemann tensor to vanish (spacetime to approach flatness) at spatial infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the natural boundary condition to select physical solutions, then noted to be powerless against flat spacetime itself.

concepts.name: uniqueness of the Einstein tensor
concepts.definition: Field equations that are generally covariant, second order in the metric and linear in T_ab can only set kappa T_ab equal to the Ricci tensor plus mu times R g_ab minus a constant Lambda times g_ab, and compatibility with nabla_b T^ab = 0 forces mu = -1/2.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated without proof after the cosmological term, as a justification that the Lambda term is the only possible addition.
concepts.notes: The rigorous result (Lovelock 1971/1972, in four dimensions) requires the left side to be a divergence-free tensor built locally from the metric and its first two derivatives; not named in the book.

concepts.name: de Sitter solution
concepts.definition: A vacuum solution of the field equations with non-zero cosmological constant, a maximally symmetric spacetime of constant curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited as a blow to the Machian hope for Lambda, since it has inertia with no matter at all.

concepts.name: dark energy
concepts.definition: A source with energy-momentum tensor proportional to the metric (constant energy density, pressure equal to minus density), obtained by moving the Lambda term to the right-hand side of the field equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the cosmological viewpoint on Lambda, deferred to the cosmology chapters.

concepts.name: Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian
concepts.definition: The Lagrangian density R sqrt(-g), plus a matter term, whose variation with respect to the metric yields the field equations; adding 2 Lambda to R gives the cosmological term.
concepts.how_introduced: Modified to (R + 2 Lambda) sqrt(-g) + 2 kappa L_M using results of Chapter 11; Hilbert's variational derivation is mentioned historically.

concepts.name: conservation of energy-momentum
concepts.definition: The vanishing covariant divergence of the energy-momentum tensor, nabla_b T^ab = 0, which follows from the field equations via the contracted Bianchi identities.
concepts.how_introduced: Checked for compatibility with Lambda in §13.3, then promoted in §13.4 to the statement that the field equations contain the equations of motion.

concepts.name: equations of motion from the field equations
concepts.definition: In general relativity the motion of matter is not an independent postulate: the conservation equations implied by the field equations force small test bodies (and dust) to follow geodesics of the metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the observation that a test particle is itself part of T_ab; historical proofs are cited, and the dust calculation serves as a model.

concepts.name: geodesic postulate
concepts.definition: The postulate that free test particles move on timelike geodesics and light rays on null geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from the axiomatic formulation of §8.5 and shown to be redundant in general relativity.
concepts.notes: The dust argument covers only timelike motion; null geodesics for light need a separate (e.g. geometric optics) argument not given.

concepts.name: dust
concepts.definition: Pressureless matter with energy-momentum tensor T^ab = rho_0 u^a u^b, where rho_0 is proper density and u^a the unit four-velocity field.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the simplest matter model for demonstrating that conservation implies geodesic flow.

concepts.name: rest-mass conservation
concepts.definition: The equation nabla_b(rho_0 u^b) = 0 stating that the flux of proper mass density is divergence free.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained as the part of the dust conservation equation along u^a, by contracting with u_a.

concepts.name: Cauchy problem
concepts.definition: The problem of constructing a solution of an evolution equation in a neighbourhood of (or to the future of) an initial hypersurface from data given on that hypersurface; for vacuum GR the data are the metric and its first time derivative on a spacelike slice.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as a boxed statement, reduced to data g_ab and g_ab,0 by noting spatial derivatives come for free, and rehearsed on the wave equation.

concepts.name: initial data
concepts.definition: The values of the unknowns and their first time derivatives on the initial hypersurface, here g_ab and g_ab,0 on Sigma_0 (subject to constraints).
concepts.how_introduced: Pared down from g_ab and all first derivatives, since tangential derivatives follow from knowing g_ab on the whole surface.

concepts.name: spacelike hypersurface
concepts.definition: A three-dimensional submanifold of spacetime all of whose tangent vectors are spacelike; here taken as x^0 = constant with x^0 a time coordinate.
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen as the carrier of initial data, drawn as a curved sheet in Figs 13.1-13.2.

concepts.name: analytic function
concepts.definition: A function equal to its convergent Taylor series in a neighbourhood of each point; its values and derivatives at one point determine it throughout its connected domain.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed so that the metric can be rebuilt from its time derivatives by Taylor series; later criticised as incompatible with causality.

concepts.name: wave equation
concepts.definition: The second-order hyperbolic equation phi_tt = phi_xx + phi_yy + phi_zz in flat spacetime (c = 1), whose Cauchy problem needs phi and phi_t on t = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Toy model for the Taylor-series construction of solutions from initial data, before tackling R_ab = 0.

concepts.name: Cauchy-Kowalevskaya theorem
concepts.definition: For a system of PDEs solved for the highest time derivatives with right-hand sides analytic in all arguments, analytic initial data determine a unique analytic solution in a neighbourhood of the initial surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Generalises the wave-equation construction; stated for second-order systems (13.16)-(13.17) with the proof idea of majorizing series.
concepts.notes: The book spells the name Kowalevskya; the standard transliteration is Kovalevskaya or Kowalevskaya.

concepts.name: majorization
concepts.definition: Proving convergence of a formal power series solution by bounding its coefficients by those of an explicitly solvable comparison problem whose analytic solution is known.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the proof sketch of Cauchy-Kowalevskaya.

concepts.name: 3+1 split of the Ricci tensor
aliases: space-time split of the vacuum equations
concepts.definition: Separating the vacuum equations into the time-time part R_00, the time-space parts R_0alpha and the space-space parts R_alphabeta with respect to a time coordinate x^0 and spatial coordinates x^alpha, and identifying which second time derivatives of the metric each contains.
concepts.how_introduced: Coordinate-component version of the 3+1 idea, used to reveal gauge freedom and constraints; the geometric version follows in Chapter 14.

concepts.name: evolution equations
concepts.definition: The six vacuum equations R_alphabeta = 0, which contain g^00 g_alphabeta,00 and so can be solved for the second time derivatives of the spatial metric, driving its evolution off the initial slice.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified as the part of the split equations in Cauchy-Kowalevskaya form once g_0a is prescribed.

concepts.name: constraint equations
concepts.definition: The four field equations G_a^0 = 0 (equivalently R_00 = 0 and R_0alpha = 0 once R_alphabeta = 0) which involve no second time derivatives after substitution and therefore restrict which initial data are allowed rather than evolving them.
concepts.how_introduced: Discovered as the over-determination problem (ten equations for six unknowns), then recast via (13.25)-(13.26).
concepts.notes: The names Hamiltonian and momentum constraints are not used here; they appear in the 3+1 language of DIV ch14.

concepts.name: over-determination of the field equations
concepts.definition: The split vacuum equations provide ten relations for only six second time derivatives g_alphabeta,00, so consistency demands compatibility conditions on the initial data.
concepts.how_introduced: Second of the two 'problems of determination' read off from (13.21)-(13.23).

concepts.name: gauge freedom in g_0a
concepts.definition: Since g_0a,00 never appears in the field equations, the four components g_0a may be specified freely near the initial slice; this choice fixes how spatial coordinates are carried forward in time and does not change the geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a 'bold step' resolving the under-determination, justified by the fourfold coordinate freedom.

concepts.name: lapse and shift
concepts.definition: The lapse measures proper time elapsed normal to the slices per unit coordinate time and the shift measures how spatial coordinates slide sideways between slices; together they encode the g_0a freedom.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the general form of choosing g_0a, deferred to §14.10.

concepts.name: Lichnerowicz normal form
aliases: normal form of the vacuum equations
concepts.definition: Writing the vacuum equations as R_alphabeta = 0 (six evolution equations) together with G_a^0 = 0 (four constraints); given R_alphabeta = 0, every other component of G_a^b is a combination of the G_a^0.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from (13.24)-(13.30) and credited to Lichnerowicz.

concepts.name: propagation of constraints
concepts.definition: If the constraints G_a^0 = 0 hold on the initial slice and the evolution equations hold everywhere, the contracted Bianchi identity gives a linear homogeneous first-order system for G_a^0, whose unique solution with zero data is zero, so the constraints hold at later times.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a 'remarkable result' and proved in the analytic setting via (13.31) and uniqueness.

concepts.name: causality objection to analyticity
concepts.definition: Analytic data are unsuitable for a causal theory because an analytic function in any small region fixes its values everywhere, whereas signals in relativity cannot outrun light; well-posedness should therefore be shown for smooth data.
concepts.how_introduced: Critique of the analytic solution just obtained, motivating Choquet-Bruhat's smooth theorem.

concepts.name: harmonic coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates whose four coordinate functions, viewed as scalar fields, each satisfy the covariant wave equation g^cd nabla_c nabla_d x^a = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen because they turn the vacuum equations into wave equations for all metric components, enabling the smooth-data existence theorem.

concepts.name: harmonic gauge condition
concepts.definition: The condition H^a := g^cd Gamma^a_cd = 0 on the contracted Christoffel symbols, equivalent to the coordinates being harmonic.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from Box x^a = 0 by a short calculation (Exercise 13.11) and shown to propagate if it holds initially.

concepts.name: reduced Einstein equations
concepts.definition: The equations R^H_ab = -1/2 g^cd g_ab,cd + Q_ab(g, dg) = 0 obtained by dropping the H_(a,b) terms from R_ab; a quasi-linear hyperbolic system for all ten metric components that agrees with the vacuum equations whenever H_a = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Via the decomposition R_ab = R^H_ab + H_(a,b), whose principal part becomes a wave operator in harmonic gauge.

concepts.name: hyperbolic partial differential equation
concepts.definition: A PDE whose highest-derivative part is a wave operator with a Lorentzian principal symbol, so that it has finite propagation speed and a well-posed Cauchy problem for smooth data.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to explain why the reduced equations can be handled by standard PDE theory while the full equations, with their gauge degeneracy, cannot.

concepts.name: propagation of the gauge condition
concepts.definition: If harmonic-gauge initial data satisfy H_a = 0 on the slice and the constraints hold, then H_a,0 also vanishes there, and the Bianchi identity gives a wave equation for H_a whose unique solution is H_a = 0, so solutions of the reduced equations solve the full vacuum equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Mirrors the constraint propagation argument of §13.6, now in the smooth setting.

concepts.name: well-posedness
concepts.definition: Existence, uniqueness (up to diffeomorphism) and continuous dependence of solutions on initial data; Choquet-Bruhat (1952) proved local existence and uniqueness for vacuum GR with smooth data (at least C^5 in the book's statement).
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the breakthrough freeing the Cauchy problem from analyticity, proved in outline with harmonic coordinates.
concepts.notes: Stability (continuous dependence) is mentioned only as an open research topic.

concepts.name: maximal globally hyperbolic development
concepts.definition: Among all vacuum spacetimes in which a given slice is a Cauchy surface carrying the prescribed data, there is a unique (up to isometry) maximal one into which every other embeds isometrically.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the global upgrade of the local smooth result.
concepts.notes: The book says 'maximal space-time' without the qualifier 'globally hyperbolic'.

concepts.name: Cauchy surface
concepts.definition: A spacelike hypersurface crossed exactly once by every inextendible causal curve, so data on it determine the whole spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Used without definition in stating the global theorem.

concepts.name: hole argument
concepts.definition: Einstein's argument that if matter outside a region H determines the metric inside, a diffeomorphism acting only inside H yields a different metric for the same matter, which seems to violate determinism unless metrics related by diffeomorphisms describe the same physical situation.
concepts.how_introduced: Revealed as a subtlety swept under the rug in setting up the Cauchy problem on a bare manifold, illustrated by Fig. 13.3.
concepts.notes: Also listed under thought_experiments. The modern reading (Earman-Norton, Stachel) treats it as an argument for diffeomorphism invariance rather than a paradox.

concepts.name: bare manifold
concepts.definition: A differentiable manifold with no metric specified; its points have no physical identity as events until a metric (and fields) are placed on it.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when making explicit the starting point of the Cauchy problem.

concepts.name: active coordinate transformation
concepts.definition: A transformation viewed as moving points of the manifold (and dragging fields along) rather than relabelling the same points.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to describe moving P to P' inside the hole.

concepts.name: spacetime as manifold plus metric
concepts.definition: A physical spacetime is a pair (M, g); two such pairs related by a diffeomorphism (coordinate transformation) are physically identical, so a physical solution is an equivalence class.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as the moral of the hole argument and already anticipated in the determinacy discussion of §13.2.
concepts.notes: The book reserves the word 'event' for a manifold point once a metric has given it physical meaning.

concepts.name: general covariance
concepts.definition: The requirement that the laws of physics take the same tensorial form in all coordinate systems, so that any coordinate transform of a solution is again a solution.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to generate the second metric in the hole argument and among the requirements leading to (13.8).

concepts.name: equivalence problem
concepts.definition: Deciding whether two given metrics are related by a coordinate transformation, i.e. whether they describe the same geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Follows naturally from defining solutions as equivalence classes in the hole problem.

concepts.name: Cartan invariants
concepts.definition: Cartan's classical solution to the equivalence problem: compare components of the Riemann tensor and its covariant derivatives (up to tenth order in the general case) in suitable frames.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as correct but computationally hopeless.

concepts.name: Karlhede algorithm
concepts.definition: A staged procedure that fixes a frame so that the Riemann tensor and successive covariant derivatives take canonical form, stopping when no new invariant information or frame freedom appears; it bounds the derivative order at seven in general and five for vacuum.
concepts.how_introduced: As the 1980 improvement making the equivalence problem computable, with practical experience that few derivatives are needed.

concepts.name: tetrad
concepts.definition: A set of four linearly independent vector fields (typically orthonormal or null) used as a basis at each point.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the device fixed stage by stage in Karlhede's method.

concepts.name: computer algebra in general relativity
concepts.definition: Symbolic manipulation software used to compute curvature, verify solutions and classify metrics invariantly, making lengthy tensor calculations feasible and reliable.
concepts.how_introduced: Through the difficulty of Riemann computations, the authors' own systems (LAM, SHEEP, CLASSI), and the printout of R_00.

concepts.name: exact solution
concepts.definition: A metric (with matter fields if any) that satisfies the field equations exactly, in closed form, rather than approximately or numerically.
concepts.how_introduced: Its prevalence, discovery methods and physical relevance are assessed in §13.2 and §13.10.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild solution
concepts.definition: The unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution, describing the exterior of a spherical mass and the simplest black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Historical surprise (January 1916) showing exact solutions exist given symmetry.

concepts.name: Birkhoff's theorem
concepts.definition: Any spherically symmetric vacuum solution is (locally) the Schwarzschild solution and hence static outside the horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Alluded to without name: the vacuum equations force spherical symmetry to imply staticity.

concepts.name: Kerr-Newman solution
concepts.definition: The exact stationary black hole solution with mass, electric charge and angular momentum.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the generalisation of Schwarzschild.

concepts.name: black hole uniqueness
concepts.definition: An isolated black hole settles down at late times to a member of the Kerr-Newman family.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited to argue that exact solutions have genuine physical value for black holes.

concepts.name: ansatz method
concepts.definition: Finding exact solutions by assuming a restricted functional form for the metric (e.g. separated variables or symmetry) and solving the simplified field equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated by Harrison's forty vacuum solutions.

concepts.name: invariant classification of metrics
concepts.definition: Characterising a geometry by coordinate-independent quantities (e.g. Karlhede invariants) so that different-looking metrics can be recognised as the same or genuinely different.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to Harrison's solutions, uncovering a duplicate; the Schwarzschild metric's roughly twenty rediscoveries show why it matters.

concepts.name: smoothness assumption
concepts.definition: The working assumption that all fields are infinitely differentiable. The minimum needed to write the field equations is a C^2 metric, so that G_ab exists; matter boundaries need weaker junction conditions.
concepts.how_introduced: Set aside in a short paragraph at the end of §13.2, with C^2 as the minimum and the Lichnerowicz conditions as the case of a surface of discontinuity. It returns in §13.6-13.7 as the contrast between analytic data and smooth data (at least C^5 in Choquet-Bruhat's theorem).

concepts.name: Einstein static universe
concepts.definition: Einstein's static, spatially closed solution for a universe uniformly filled with matter, which exists only when the cosmological term is included.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as Einstein's attempt to build a model universe that would supply Machian boundary conditions. It forced the Lambda term into the equations and was abandoned once cosmic expansion was found.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the name; it speaks of a static closed solution. Treated in the cosmology chapters.

key_equations.name: Einstein field equations
key_equations.meaning: Curvature (Einstein tensor) equals 8 pi times energy-momentum, in units G = c = 1; the object of study throughout the chapter.
key_equations.symbols: G_ab Einstein tensor; T_ab energy-momentum tensor

key_equations.name: Vacuum field equations
key_equations.meaning: Ten equations for ten metric components in empty regions; the case analysed in the Cauchy problem.

key_equations.name: Contracted Bianchi identities
key_equations.meaning: Four identities holding for every metric, so the ten field equations are not independent.

key_equations.name: General coordinate transformation
key_equations.meaning: Four arbitrary functions of freedom, matching the four identities; metrics related this way are the same geometry.

key_equations.name: Gaussian normal coordinate conditions
key_equations.meaning: Example of four gauge conditions; the remaining six g_alphabeta are left for six independent equations.
key_equations.symbols: starred equality holds in the chosen coordinates only; alpha = 1,2,3

key_equations.name: Field equations with cosmological term
key_equations.meaning: Einstein's 1917 modification; the sign reflects the book's (+,-,-,-) signature, so Lambda > 0 is still repulsive.

key_equations.name: Metric compatibility
key_equations.meaning: The metric is covariantly constant, so the Lambda term has zero divergence and does not spoil conservation.

key_equations.name: Conservation equations
key_equations.meaning: Consistency requirement on the source, implied by the Bianchi identities with or without Lambda.

key_equations.name: Lagrangian with cosmological term
key_equations.meaning: Varying this density with respect to the metric gives (13.5) (Exercise 13.1).
key_equations.symbols: R Ricci scalar; g metric determinant; kappa coupling constant; L_M matter Lagrangian

key_equations.name: Most general admissible field equation
key_equations.meaning: Form forced by general covariance, second order and linearity in T; conservation then fixes mu = -1/2 (Exercise 13.2).

key_equations.name: Conservation equations (from Bianchi identities)
key_equations.meaning: Restated in §13.4 as the carrier of the equations of motion of matter.

key_equations.name: Dust energy-momentum tensor
key_equations.meaning: Pressureless matter used in the geodesic-motion demonstration.

key_equations.name: Leibniz expansion of dust conservation
key_equations.meaning: Splits the divergence into a mass-flux part along u and an acceleration part.

key_equations.name: Normalisation implies orthogonal acceleration
key_equations.meaning: Contracting (13.10) with u_a kills the second term.

key_equations.name: Rest-mass conservation
key_equations.meaning: Continuity equation for proper mass.

key_equations.name: Geodesic equation for dust
key_equations.meaning: Result: dust worldlines are geodesics as a consequence of the field equations.

key_equations.name: Initial data for the vacuum Cauchy problem
key_equations.meaning: Metric potentials and their time derivatives suffice because spatial derivatives follow from g_ab on the slice.

key_equations.name: Taylor expansion of the metric off the slice
key_equations.meaning: If all time derivatives at P on Sigma_0 are known, an analytic metric is reconstructed at Q along the x^0 coordinate line.

key_equations.name: Flat wave equation
key_equations.meaning: Model problem: phi and phi_t on t = 0 should determine a unique solution.

key_equations.name: Time derivative of the wave equation
key_equations.latex: \frac{\partial^3\phi}{\partial t^3} = \frac{\partial^3\phi}{\partial t\,\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^3\phi}{\partial t\,\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^3\phi}{\partial t\,\partial z^2}
key_equations.meaning: Spatial derivatives of the given phi_t on the slice yield phi_ttt.

key_equations.name: Second time derivative of the wave equation
key_equations.latex: \frac{\partial^4\phi}{\partial t^4} = \frac{\partial^4\phi}{\partial t^2\,\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^4\phi}{\partial t^2\,\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^4\phi}{\partial t^2\,\partial z^2}
key_equations.meaning: Spatial derivatives of the already-known phi_tt give phi_tttt; the pattern continues to all orders. Printed correctly in the book; the text export garbles the first term.

key_equations.name: Taylor-series solution of the wave equation
key_equations.meaning: The solution is assembled from all time derivatives at t = 0 and is valid where the series converges, which analytic data guarantee. The 1/n! is restored here because the printed equation omits it.

key_equations.name: Cauchy-Kowalevskaya system
key_equations.meaning: Second-order system solved for the second time derivatives with an analytic right-hand side. The book calls this function F^A, while the text export misreads it as P^A. As printed, the argument list omits first time derivatives of Phi^B.
key_equations.symbols: Phi^A, A = 1..N unknowns; F^A analytic functions; x in R^n

key_equations.name: Analytic Cauchy data
key_equations.meaning: Given analytic P^A, Q^A, (13.16) has a unique analytic solution near t = 0.

key_equations.name: Split vacuum equations
key_equations.meaning: Time-time, time-space and space-space parts of R_ab = 0 relative to a time coordinate x^0 with g^00 > 0.

key_equations.name: R_00 in terms of second time derivatives
key_equations.meaning: Only the trace of g_alphabeta,00 appears; M_00 is fixed by initial data.
key_equations.symbols: M_ab: terms computable from g_ab, g_ab,0 and their spatial derivatives on Sigma_0

key_equations.name: R_0alpha in terms of second time derivatives
key_equations.meaning: Again only g_alphabeta,00 appears, contracted with g^0beta.

key_equations.name: Evolution equations
key_equations.meaning: Solvable for g_alphabeta,00 since g^00 is non-zero: six equations for six unknowns in Cauchy-Kowalevskaya form once g_0a is prescribed.

key_equations.name: Ricci scalar when R_alphabeta = 0
key_equations.meaning: Trace reduces to the constraint components.

key_equations.name: G_0^0 as a constraint
key_equations.meaning: With R_alphabeta = 0, R_00 = 0 is equivalent to G_0^0 = 0.

key_equations.name: G_alpha^0 as a constraint
key_equations.meaning: With R_alphabeta = 0, R_0alpha = 0 is equivalent to G_alpha^0 = 0.

key_equations.name: Spatial Einstein components
key_equations.meaning: Vanishes once the constraint components vanish.

key_equations.name: Mixed Einstein components
key_equations.meaning: Also vanishes once R_00 and R_0lambda vanish.

key_equations.name: G_0^beta in terms of constraints
key_equations.meaning: Given R_alphabeta = 0, every remaining Einstein component is linear in the constraint quantities G_a^0.

key_equations.name: G_alpha^beta in terms of constraints
key_equations.meaning: Companion to (13.29); both substituted into the Bianchi identity.

key_equations.name: Lichnerowicz normal form
key_equations.meaning: Six evolution equations plus four constraints on the initial data.

key_equations.name: Bianchi identity as evolution of the constraints
key_equations.meaning: After substituting (13.29)-(13.30), a linear homogeneous first-order system for G_a^0; zero data give zero solution, so constraints propagate.

key_equations.name: Harmonic coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Each coordinate function is a solution of the curved wave equation.

key_equations.name: Harmonic gauge condition
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent algebraic-differential form of (13.32) (Exercise 13.11), since Box x^a = -g^cd Gamma^a_cd.

key_equations.name: Ricci decomposition
key_equations.meaning: Separates the gauge-dependent part (derivatives of H_a) from a part with wave-operator principal term.
key_equations.symbols: H_a = g_ab H^b; parentheses denote symmetrisation

key_equations.name: Reduced Ricci tensor
key_equations.meaning: Principal part is the wave operator acting on each metric component; Q contains at most first derivatives.
key_equations.symbols: Q_ab depends on g_ab, g^ab, g_ab,c

key_equations.name: Reduced Einstein equations
key_equations.meaning: Quasi-linear hyperbolic system for all ten g_ab, well posed for smooth data; equals vacuum GR when H_a = 0.

key_equations.name: Constraints with g_00 = 1, g_0alpha = 0 on the slice
key_equations.meaning: Solved on Sigma_0 for the spatial metric gamma_alphabeta = -g_alphabeta and K_alphabeta = g_alphabeta,0.
key_equations.symbols: gamma_alphabeta positive-definite 3-metric; K_alphabeta time derivative of spatial metric

key_equations.name: Initial harmonic gauge
key_equations.meaning: Achieved by choosing g_0b,0 on the slice (Exercise 13.12); with constraints, H_a,0 = 0 also, so H_a = 0 persists.

key_equations.name: Exercise 13.5 perfect fluid conservation
key_equations.meaning: Relativistic Euler equation: pressure gradients orthogonal to u cause deviation from geodesic motion.

figures.label: Fig. 13.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Where the Cauchy initial data live: the metric and its time derivative prescribed on the initial slice.
figures.visual_description: A single wavy, sheet-like quadrilateral drawn in perspective, labelled S in its lower-left corner. A leader line from the right edge carries the label x^0 = 0. In the middle of the sheet the word 'Prescribe' is followed by a brace enclosing g_ab above g_ab,0. No axes, no time direction, no normals are drawn.
figures.what_it_teaches: The initial value problem starts from a 3-surface of constant time on which only the metric and its first time derivative are specified.

redesign.idea: 3D slice-stacking view: a warped translucent sheet Sigma_0 carries a colour map of a chosen metric component and small arrows for its time derivative; the learner watches later slices being generated upward only after the data pass a constraint check.
redesign.interaction: Paint g_alphabeta and g_alphabeta,0 on the sheet with brushes; a constraint meter turns green only when the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints (for a simple conformally flat family) are satisfied; a 'evolve' button stacks subsequent slices.

figures.label: Fig. 13.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Reconstructing the metric at a later coordinate time by following a time coordinate line off the slice.
figures.visual_description: The same wavy sheet labelled S and x^0 = 0. A dot P sits on the sheet; a thick slightly curved line rises from P up through the top edge of the sheet to a second dot Q above it. A leader line labels this curve x^alpha = x_0^alpha, i.e. the spatial coordinates are held fixed along it.
figures.what_it_teaches: Values of the metric at Q are built from derivatives at P via a Taylor series in x^0 along a curve of constant spatial coordinates, which is why all time derivatives on the slice are needed and why analyticity enters.

redesign.idea: Taylor-series tower: a 1D analogue where a curve phi(t) above a point P is approximated by successive Taylor polynomials built from derivatives at P, alongside a 2D wave-equation version where the learner sees the derivatives generated by the equation.
redesign.interaction: Slider for the number of Taylor terms and for x^0; toggle between analytic data (series converges) and a smooth bump function with compact support (series fails to reproduce it), dramatising the causality objection.

figures.label: Fig. 13.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Einstein's hole argument: matter known outside a hole, points inside it moved.
figures.visual_description: Two side-by-side irregular blobs, each diagonally hatched (the region where the matter distribution is known, labelled by a shared caption with leader lines to both). Each blob contains an unhatched interior region labelled H. In the left hole a single dot P. In the right hole two dots, P above and P' below, joined by a short arrow indicating that the point has been displaced within the hole while everything in the hatched region is unchanged.
figures.what_it_teaches: A transformation that is the identity outside H but shifts points inside H gives a metric of different functional form with identical exterior matter; the apparent indeterminism dissolves once bare points are recognised as having no physical identity.

redesign.idea: Rubber-grid hole demo: a 2D grid with a hatched outer ring and a hole; inside, a field pattern (e.g. contour lines of a curvature scalar) and a marked point P. The learner drags a smooth deformation inside the hole only. The component plot g_xx(x, y) changes, but a panel of invariants (curvature scalar at events defined by intersections of physical fields) is unchanged.
redesign.interaction: Drag handles to deform the interior; toggle 'label by coordinates' versus 'label by physical landmarks' to see that coordinate-labelled values change while landmark-labelled values do not.

figures.label: Fig. 13.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Computer-algebra printout of the opening 26 terms of R_00 for a completely general metric.
figures.visual_description: A block of monospaced line-printer output (no exported image; described from the rendered page). It begins 'R_00 = 1/4 G00 G11 G22 g ...' with exponents such as 2 and -2 printed on a raised line above the symbols and derivative subscripts such as ,Z ,T ,Y printed on a lowered line below. Each of about thirteen lines holds two terms, each term a rational coefficient (1/4, 1/2, 1) times products of powers of metric components G00, G11, G22, G23, G33, the inverse-square of the determinant g, and products of two first derivatives of metric components, ending with a trailing plus sign to show the sum continues.
figures.what_it_teaches: Visceral evidence that the field equations, written without any symmetry, are enormous (order 10^5 terms in R_ab), explaining why exact solutions require symmetry and why computer algebra is indispensable.

redesign.idea: Symmetry-collapse counter: start from a live symbolic count of the terms in R_00 for a general metric, then let the learner switch on assumptions (diagonal metric, static, spherically symmetric, vacuum) and watch the term count and the displayed expression shrink to the familiar Schwarzschild ODEs.
redesign.interaction: Checkboxes for each assumption; a log-scale bar shows term count; clicking a term highlights which metric functions it involves.

worked_examples.problem: Show that the conservation equations for dust force each dust particle to move on a geodesic.
worked_examples.method: Write the divergence of rho_0 u^a u^b as a product rule on (rho_0 u^b) and u^a; contract with u_a and use that the derivative of the unit normalisation makes u_a nabla_b u^a vanish; deduce the continuity equation; substitute back and divide by non-zero rho_0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Projecting the conservation law along and orthogonal to the four-velocity separates mass conservation from the equation of motion; with no pressure there is no force term, so the orthogonal part is the geodesic equation.
worked_examples.result: nabla_b(rho_0 u^b) = 0 and u^b nabla_b u^a = 0.
concepts: equations of motion from the field equations

worked_examples.problem: Construct the solution of the flat wave equation from analytic data phi and phi_t on t = 0.
worked_examples.method: Use the equation to convert spatial derivatives of phi into phi_tt on the slice; differentiate the equation in t repeatedly so each new time derivative is given by spatial derivatives of an already-known one; assemble the Taylor series in t and bound it using analyticity (even coefficients from phi, odd from phi_t).
worked_examples.key_insight: A second-order evolution equation turns two functions on a slice into all time derivatives; convergence is the only issue, and analyticity settles it.
worked_examples.result: phi(t, x) = sum_n (1/n!) d^n phi/dt^n (0, x) t^n; in fact the even terms are powers of the Laplacian acting on phi(0, x).

worked_examples.problem: Determine which second time derivatives of the metric appear in the vacuum equations and what this implies for determinacy.
worked_examples.method: Split R_ab = 0 into 00, 0alpha, alphabeta parts, isolate terms in g_ab,00 (13.21)-(13.23), collect everything else into M_ab computable from the data, and count unknowns versus equations.
worked_examples.key_insight: g_0a,00 never appears (gauge freedom) while ten equations involve only six g_alphabeta,00 (four constraints).
worked_examples.result: Prescribe g_0a; solve R_alphabeta = 0 for g_alphabeta,00; the other four equations restrict the data.

worked_examples.problem: Assuming R_alphabeta = 0, show that R_00 = 0 and R_0alpha = 0 are equivalent to G_a^0 = 0, and that G_a^0 = 0 implies all of G_a^b = 0.
worked_examples.method: Compute R from the surviving components (13.24); evaluate G_0^0 and G_alpha^0 (13.25)-(13.26); write G_alpha^beta and G_0^beta in terms of R_00, R_0alpha (13.27)-(13.28); invert to express them through G_a^0 (13.29)-(13.30).
worked_examples.key_insight: Once the evolution equations hold, the whole Einstein tensor is a linear function of the four constraint quantities, so controlling G_a^0 controls everything.

worked_examples.problem: Prove that constraints satisfied on the initial slice remain satisfied under evolution by R_alphabeta = 0.
worked_examples.method: Expand nabla_b G_a^b = 0 in coordinates to isolate partial_t G_a^0 (13.31); substitute (13.29)-(13.30) so the right side is linear and homogeneous in G_a^0 and its spatial derivatives; apply Cauchy-Kowalevskaya uniqueness with zero initial data.
worked_examples.key_insight: A linear homogeneous evolution system with zero data has only the zero solution: the Bianchi identity is a built-in constraint-preserving mechanism.
worked_examples.result: G_a^0 = 0 near Sigma_0, hence the full vacuum equations hold.

worked_examples.problem: Outline how smooth solutions of the vacuum equations are obtained using harmonic coordinates.
worked_examples.method: Decompose R_ab into R^H_ab plus derivatives of H_a; solve constraints on Sigma_0 with g_00 = 1, g_0alpha = 0; choose g_0b,0 so H_a = 0 initially; use constraints to get H_a,0 = 0; show via the Bianchi identity that H_a obeys a wave equation and hence stays zero; solve the hyperbolic reduced equations.
worked_examples.key_insight: Gauge fixing converts a degenerate system into a genuinely hyperbolic one, and the same Bianchi-identity trick guarantees the gauge (and thus the true equations) is preserved.
worked_examples.result: Local existence and uniqueness for smooth data (Choquet-Bruhat 1952).

worked_examples.problem: Count equations and unknowns for the vacuum field equations.
worked_examples.method: Ten symmetric equations for ten metric components, reduced by four differential identities; compensated by four arbitrary coordinate functions; impose four gauge conditions such as Gaussian normal coordinates, leaving six unknowns for six independent equations.
worked_examples.key_insight: The apparent under-determination is exactly the coordinate freedom, so solutions are unique only as geometries.
worked_examples.result: 6 physical equations for the 6 components g_alphabeta in Gaussian normal gauge (with a caveat resolved in §13.6).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Gravitational field energy as its own source
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The field of a source carries energy, hence mass by E = mc^2, which itself gravitates, so the field couples to itself and solutions cannot simply be added.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Gravitational energy is not locally definable in GR; the argument is heuristic.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Show two point-mass potentials added linearly versus a numerically solved non-linear field (e.g. Brill-Lindquist vs naive sum) with a difference heatmap.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Lichnerowicz junction conditions as the continuity conditions of Newtonian potential theory
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Just as the Newtonian potential and its gradient stay continuous across a body's surface while its second derivatives jump with density, the metric and its first derivatives are continuous across a surface of discontinuity.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The GR conditions are coordinate dependent as stated; covariant (Israel-Darmois) versions use induced metric and extrinsic curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Plot Phi, Phi' and Phi'' for a uniform sphere, showing the jump only in Phi'' at the surface.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Solving the wave equation by Taylor series as a rehearsal for the Einstein Cauchy problem
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The same steps (use the equation to get second time derivatives, differentiate to get higher ones, sum the series) are carried out on a simple linear equation first.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The wave equation has no gauge freedom or constraints; those are exactly the new features of GR.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side 'recipe cards' for the wave equation and R_ab = 0 with the steps that fail for GR highlighted.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Lambda as a Newtonian cosmic repulsion felt by all matter
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: In Newtonian cosmology a positive Lambda produces a universal outward force, negative Lambda an attraction, a long-range Machian-like interaction.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In GR Lambda is a property of spacetime (vacuum energy) and its effect grows with distance, not as a force between bodies.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Particles in an expanding ball with slider for Lambda showing acceleration a = (Lambda/3) r added to Newtonian attraction.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Moving Lambda from the geometry side to the matter side as dark energy
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The same term can be read as a modification of gravity or as a source with T_ab proportional to g_ab.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Equivalent only for a strict constant; dynamical dark energy is different.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Stack of printed paper about 3 m high
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The roughly 100,000 terms of the general Ricci tensor, printed on A4, would form a pile three metres tall, making the complexity tangible.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Term count depends on how the determinant and inverse metric are expanded.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Animated stack growing next to a human silhouette as symmetry assumptions are removed.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Unlabelled points on a bare manifold as seats without tickets
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Not in the book (added intuition): moving a point P inside the hole is meaningless until the metric gives events identity, just as a seat number has no meaning until someone is assigned to it.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Informal; manifold points do have topological structure.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Given any matter distribution, the field equations determine a unique metric.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Matter determines the geometry only up to coordinate transformations and, beyond that, also depends on boundary and initial conditions; the equations are not fully Machian.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Ten equations for ten unknowns looks well posed, and the Poisson-equation analogy suggests source uniquely fixes field.
concepts: three readings of the field equations

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any metric you write down is a valid solution because you can just compute the T_ab it needs.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Formally yes, but the resulting matter almost always has negative energy density or otherwise violates the energy conditions, so it is not physical.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The equations can be read left to right mechanically.
concepts: three readings of the field equations

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since solutions are not unique, the theory is indeterministic.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The non-uniqueness is exactly diffeomorphism freedom; metrics related by coordinate transformations are the same physical spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Different component functions look like different fields; the hole argument initially convinced Einstein of this.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: You can add two gravitational solutions to get the field of both sources together.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The equations are non-linear, so there is no superposition principle; only in the linearized approximation does adding work.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian gravity and electromagnetism are linear.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Geodesic motion is an extra postulate that must be added to Einstein's equations.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The field equations imply conservation, which forces geodesic motion for test matter (shown explicitly for dust).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Many courses state the geodesic postulate and the field equations as separate axioms, as in the special relativity axioms of §8.5.
concepts: equations of motion from the field equations

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: All ten metric components are evolved by the field equations from initial data.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the six spatial components have dynamical second time derivatives; g_0a is gauge and is chosen, and four equations are constraints on the data.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Counting ten equations for ten unknowns.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Initial data for GR can be chosen freely.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The data must satisfy the four constraint equations on the slice, which is itself a non-trivial elliptic problem.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: For the wave equation any phi and phi_t are allowed.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Enforcing the constraints at every time step is a separate requirement in the evolution.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: If they hold initially and the evolution equations hold, the Bianchi identity guarantees they continue to hold (in the exact theory; numerically they drift).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Constraints look like independent equations that could be violated later.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An analytic existence theorem is physically adequate.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Analytic functions are fixed everywhere by any small patch, contradicting causality; physically meaningful well-posedness needs smooth data, achieved in harmonic gauge.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Cauchy-Kowalevskaya gives existence and uniqueness neatly.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Adding Lambda makes general relativity Machian.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It removes Minkowski space as a solution, but de Sitter space is a matter-free solution with Lambda, so inertia without matter persists.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Two metrics that look different describe different spacetimes.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They may be related by a coordinate change; only invariant classification (Cartan-Karlhede) settles it, as with the repeated rediscovery of Schwarzschild and the duplicate among Harrison's solutions.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Metric components are the most visible description.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Having thousands of exact solutions means GR's important problems are solved exactly.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Most exact solutions have singularities or other unphysical features, and none is known for the two-body problem, for black hole interiors, or for radiation from an isolated source, so approximation methods and numerical relativity are needed.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The large catalogue of Kramer et al.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Setting g_00 = 1 and g_0alpha = 0 is a physical assumption about the spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is a coordinate choice (Gaussian normal gauge), always possible locally near a spacelike slice, though such coordinates may break down later where geodesics cross.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It looks like assuming a static or synchronous universe.

thought_experiments.name: Einstein's hole argument
thought_experiments.setup: Matter is known everywhere outside a region H of a bare manifold; the field equations fix the metric inside. Apply a transformation that is trivial outside H but slides a point P to P' inside, and recompute the metric in H.
thought_experiments.lesson: The new metric has different component functions but is the same physical solution, because manifold points have no identity apart from the metric; spacetimes are equivalence classes under diffeomorphism.
thought_experiments.app_idea: See Fig. 13.3 redesign: deform the hole interior and compare coordinate-labelled versus invariant-labelled readings.

thought_experiments.name: A lone test body in an empty universe
thought_experiments.setup: Consider a single test body in a universe with no other matter, described by Minkowski space as a vacuum solution.
thought_experiments.lesson: The body would have inertia with nothing to produce it, which Einstein took as a violation of Mach's principle and part of his reason to introduce Lambda.

thought_experiments.name: The test particle as part of the source
thought_experiments.setup: Instead of placing a test particle on a given geometry, include it in T_ab so it helps create the geometry it moves in.
thought_experiments.lesson: The motion must then be encoded in the field equations themselves, via the conservation law; geodesic motion is a consequence, not an axiom.
concepts: equations of motion from the field equations
thought_experiments.app_idea: Dust cloud simulation where turning pressure to zero makes flow lines coincide with overlaid geodesics, and non-zero pressure makes them deviate.

thought_experiments.name: Designer metric
thought_experiments.setup: Pick ten arbitrary functions for g_ab, compute G_ab, and read off the matter needed.
thought_experiments.lesson: Generically the matter has negative energy density somewhere, so physical content lies in the energy conditions, not in the equations alone.
concepts: three readings of the field equations
thought_experiments.app_idea: Metric sandbox: learner sketches g_tt(r) and g_rr(r) for a static spherical metric; the app shows the implied rho(r) and p(r) and shades regions violating energy conditions red.

historical_notes.event: Found the first exact solution of the field equations (static, spherically symmetric vacuum) in January 1916, a little over a month after the equations were published.
historical_notes.significance: Overturned Einstein's expectation that exact solutions would be unattainable and showed the power of symmetry assumptions.

historical_notes.event: Introduced the cosmological term to obtain a static, closed, homogeneous universe, then abandoned it after cosmic expansion was established, reportedly calling it his biggest blunder.
historical_notes.significance: Explains the origin and changing fortunes of Lambda, now reinterpreted as dark energy.

historical_notes.event: Derived the field equations from a variational principle in the same year as Einstein.
historical_notes.significance: Origin of the Lagrangian formulation; the book stresses Einstein supplied the physical grounding via the equivalence principle.

historical_notes.event: Found a vacuum solution of the field equations with a cosmological term.
historical_notes.significance: Undermined the idea that Lambda makes GR Machian.

historical_notes.event: Showed, by treating particles as field singularities, that the field equations determine the equations of motion of bodies.
historical_notes.significance: Established that geodesic motion need not be postulated separately; later confirmed rigorously by Geroch and Jang and by Gralla and Wald.

historical_notes.event: Proved local existence and uniqueness of solutions to the vacuum Einstein equations for smooth (at least C^5) initial data using harmonic coordinates.
historical_notes.significance: Established GR as a well-posed causal evolution theory independent of analyticity.

historical_notes.event: Proved existence and uniqueness of a maximal development of vacuum initial data.
historical_notes.significance: Global counterpart of the local theorem (published 1969; year not given in the book).

historical_notes.event: Formulated the vacuum equations in normal form (evolution plus constraints) and junction conditions across surfaces of discontinuity.
historical_notes.significance: Precursor of the 3+1 formalism used in numerical relativity.

historical_notes.event: Einstein's hole argument troubled him for years before the final field equations; Stachel (2001) summarised its resolution with the slogan that without a metric there is nothing.
historical_notes.significance: Clarified that general covariance forces points to be individuated by the metric; the book dates Einstein's general covariance ideas to 1907 and says eight more years passed.

historical_notes.event: Cartan solved the equivalence problem in principle; Karlhede (1980) made it computable; Ramos and Vickers (1996) lowered the vacuum bound to fifth derivatives.
historical_notes.significance: Made invariant classification of exact solutions practical with computer algebra. Dates: Karlhede 1980, Ramos and Vickers 1996; Cartan's work is much earlier and is not dated in the book.

historical_notes.event: Wrote out the general field equations explicitly for the first time using his Lisp-based computer algebra system LAM, later succeeded by SHEEP.
historical_notes.significance: Early landmark of computer algebra in relativity; also used to verify Harrison's solutions.

historical_notes.event: Found forty vacuum solutions with a separation-of-variables ansatz; later computer classification showed two were the same.
historical_notes.significance: Illustrates both ansatz methods and the need for invariant classification. The book dates the work to 1955; Harrison's Physical Review paper on these solutions appeared in 1959, so check the date before quoting it.

applications_and_observations.topic: Numerical relativity waveforms for gravitational-wave detection
applications_and_observations.details: Simulations of colliding black holes, based on the 3+1 split of the field equations, supplied template waveforms essential to detecting gravitational waves.
The discovery that the universe expands, from the redshifts of galaxies, removed Einstein's motive for a static universe and for Lambda.

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of the general Ricci tensor
applications_and_observations.details: Fully expanded for an arbitrary metric, with the determinant kept as a symbol, the Ricci tensor contains of order a hundred thousand terms; printed on A4 it would stack about three metres high.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: ~1e5 terms; ~3 m of paper; Fig. 13.4 shows 26 terms of R_00

applications_and_observations.topic: Derivative order needed for invariant classification
applications_and_observations.details: Cartan's method needs up to the tenth covariant derivative of Riemann; Karlhede's algorithm at worst the seventh, the fifth for vacuum; in practice usually third or less, often first.

Known exact solutions number in the thousands, catalogued in Kramer et al.; Harrison's ansatz alone gave forty vacuum solutions, two of which turned out identical; Schwarzschild's metric was published as new about twenty times.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: thousands of solutions; 40 Harrison solutions (39 distinct); ~20 rediscoveries of Schwarzschild

applications_and_observations.topic: Isolated black holes settle to Kerr-Newman
applications_and_observations.details: An isolated black hole approaches the Kerr-Newman family at late times, so an exact solution describes the end state of realistic collapse.

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of Lambda in local physics (own estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Not in the book: taking the observed Lambda as about 1.1e-52 m^-2, the extra acceleration Lambda c^2 r/3 at 1 AU comes to about 5e-25 m/s^2. The Sun's pull there is about 6e-3 m/s^2, which justifies the book's neglect of Lambda in solar system physics.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Lambda ~ 1.1e-52 m^-2; a_Lambda ~ 5e-25 m/s^2 at 1 AU; ratio ~ 1e-22 (own estimate)

notation_and_conventions.convention: Metric signature (+,-,-,-): x^0 timelike means g^00 > 0, Gaussian normal coordinates have g_00 = +1, and the spatial 3-metric is gamma_alphabeta = -g_alphabeta (positive definite).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Readers coming from (-,+,+,+) texts must flip signs of g_ab and gamma.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Latin indices a, b, ... run 0-3; Greek indices alpha, beta, ... run 1-3 (spatial).
notation_and_conventions.notes: The Exercise 13.8 hint splits Latin sums into 0 and Greek parts.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Comma denotes partial derivative (g_ab,0 = partial_0 g_ab); semicolon or nabla denotes covariant derivative.
An equals sign with an asterisk marks relations valid only in a particular coordinate system, e.g. Gaussian normal coordinates.
G = c = 1 so the coupling is 8 pi; kappa denotes the general coupling constant in (13.7)-(13.8).

The book writes G_ab - Lambda g_ab = 8 pi T_ab 'with our sign conventions', i.e. signature (+,-,-,-). With signature (-,+,+,+) and the same Ricci convention, g_ab changes sign while G_ab and T_ab do not, so the same physics is written G_ab + Lambda g_ab = 8 pi T_ab (as in MTW).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Positive Lambda is repulsive in both.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The initial hypersurface is called Sigma_0 in the text and S in Figs 13.1-13.2 and Exercises 13.6, 13.10; Sigma_t denotes x^0 = t slices.
M_ab collects all terms of the split Ricci components not containing g_ab,00; Q_ab collects the terms of R^H_ab with no second derivatives.
H^a = g^cd Gamma^a_cd is the harmonic gauge quantity; H_a its index-lowered form; R^H_ab the reduced Ricci tensor; round brackets on indices denote symmetrisation.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The book switches between upper and lower H without comment.

notation_and_conventions.convention: G_a^b with the constraint quantities written G_a^0 and the relation G_a^b = R_a^b - (1/2) delta_a^b R.
Defined here simply as g_alphabeta,0 on Sigma_0 in the gauge g_00 = 1, g_0alpha = 0.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Proportional to, but not normalised or signed as, the extrinsic curvature used in Chapter 14.

notation_and_conventions.convention: G00...G33 denote metric components, T, X, Y, Z the coordinates, ',Z' partial derivatives, and g the determinant kept as a symbol.

margin_notes.summary: The Cauchy problem is stated in a shaded box as the task of building the whole future spacetime from the metric and its first derivatives on one time slice.

Shaded boxes highlight the initial data (g_ab, g_ab,0), the Lichnerowicz normal form, the harmonic gauge condition, the reduced equations, and the statement that constraints hold for all time once satisfied initially.
Forward pointers: lapse and shift in §14.10, solving the constraints in §14.12, a geometric treatment showing all solutions arise this way in Chapter 14.
Humorous aside that SHEEP is LAM grown up, noting the lineage of the authors' computer algebra systems.

Exercise 13.13 is an optional practical exercise on getting access to computer algebra, noting SHEEP is freely available and pointing to MacCallum's Living Reviews article on computer algebra in gravity research.
Further reading: the Cauchy problem treatment follows Adler-Bazin-Schiffer and Wald; Ringstrom for full detail; d'Inverno (1980) for algebraic computing; Kramer et al. for exact solutions.

notable.summary: Show the electromagnetic stress tensor is traceless, find which mu makes both sides of (13.8) traceless when Lambda = 0, and use it to suggest an alternative coupling of gravity to Maxwell fields.
notable.why_notable: Invites the reader to invent and then test a rival theory against the conservation requirement (mu = -1/4 would conflict with nabla T = 0 in general), sharpening why mu = -1/2 is forced.

notable.summary: From conservation for a perfect fluid, derive the relativistic Euler equation; then for a barotropic fluid build a rescaled velocity C_a = f u_a with f an exponential of a pressure integral, form its curl Omega_ab, and show C^a Omega_ab = 0.

notable.summary: Derive the component forms (13.21)-(13.23) of the vacuum equations, isolating second time derivatives.

notable.summary: Establish the coordinate form of the Bianchi identity for G_a^0, show it becomes a homogeneous first-order system with coefficients depending only on the metric and its first derivatives, and use a formal power series to show vanishing on the slice implies vanishing everywhere.
notable.why_notable: Makes the 'remarkable result' of §13.6 fully explicit.

notable.summary: Show harmonic coordinates satisfy g^cd Gamma^a_cd = 0, treating each coordinate function as a scalar labelled by a.
notable.why_notable: The hint addresses a genuine conceptual trap: x^a for fixed a is a scalar, not a vector component.

notable.summary: Given constraint-satisfying spatial data, choose the time derivatives of g_0b on the slice to make H^a vanish there, using H^0 = 0 for g_00,0 and H^alpha = 0 for g_0alpha,0.
notable.why_notable: Completes the smooth existence argument of §13.7.

difficulty.notes: The discursive sections (13.1-13.4, 13.8-13.10) are accessible and historically rich, but §13.5-13.7 introduce PDE theory (analyticity, Cauchy-Kowalevskaya, hyperbolicity, majorants) with key calculations left as exercises and several results quoted. Index gymnastics in (13.24)-(13.31) are dense, and the smooth harmonic-gauge proof is only sketched. Conceptually, gauge freedom versus physical content, constraints versus evolution, and the hole argument are among the subtlest ideas in GR. A few printed slips (the missing 1/n! in (13.15), the integrand in Exercise 13.5) and stale section pointers add friction.

teaching_gems.gem: Balance sheet of ten equations, four identities, four coordinate functions, six evolution equations and four constraints.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns an abstract well-posedness question into bookkeeping learners can reproduce and check, and it recurs in every later formalism (3+1, gauge choices in numerics).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive ledger: ten tiles for metric components and ten for equations; learner drags 'Bianchi identity' and 'coordinate freedom' tokens to cancel tiles, ending with six dynamical pairs and four constraint tiles attached to the initial slice.

teaching_gems.gem: Rehearse the Cauchy construction on the flat wave equation before GR.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners see derivatives being generated from data in a setting with no index clutter, so the only new ideas in GR are gauge and constraints.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Live Taylor builder for a 1D wave: learner edits phi(0,x) and phi_t(0,x); the app shows successive time-derivative profiles and the partial sums converging toward the d'Alembert solution.

teaching_gems.gem: Dust conservation to geodesic motion in four lines using the Leibniz rule and u_a nabla u^a = 0.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A compact, fully checkable proof that 'matter tells itself how to move', demystifying a result whose historical proofs were enormous.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-through derivation card with each line animated as a projection: parallel to u (continuity) and perpendicular to u (acceleration), with a pressure slider adding the Euler term from Exercise 13.5.

teaching_gems.gem: Locate the second time derivatives: only g_alphabeta,00 appears, exposing gauge (missing g_0a,00) and constraints (surplus equations) in one move.
teaching_gems.why_effective: One diagnostic reveals both structural features of GR as an evolution system.
teaching_gems.app_idea: 10x10 matrix heatmap of which g_ab,00 appears in which R_ab equation, computed symbolically for a generic metric; rows R_00 and R_0alpha light up only through g_alphabeta,00 combinations.

teaching_gems.gem: Constraints are preserved because their evolution equation is linear and homogeneous: zero stays zero.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives a simple mental model (a homogeneous ODE with zero data) for a deep consequence of the Bianchi identity, and connects directly to constraint-violation growth in numerical relativity.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Toy evolution of a constraint quantity dC/dt = A C: exact zero data stays at zero, while a tiny numerical error grows or decays depending on a damping parameter, previewing constraint damping.

teaching_gems.gem: Analyticity violates causality because an analytic function is known everywhere from a small patch.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A crisp physical argument for why mathematicians needed a harder (smooth, hyperbolic) theorem.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Compare an analytic pulse and a compactly supported bump initial profile; show that the bump's Taylor series at the origin is identically zero while the true wave arrives later, respecting the light cone.

teaching_gems.gem: Printout of the first 26 terms of R_00 and the three-metre paper stack.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes the scale of the equations tangible and motivates symmetry, approximation, numerics and computer algebra in one picture.
teaching_gems.app_idea: See Fig. 13.4 redesign: toggle symmetry assumptions and watch the term count collapse.

teaching_gems.gem: The hole argument resolved by 'no metric, no nothing': points get identity only from the metric.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Addresses head-on the most common philosophical confusion about general covariance and ties together determinacy, gauge and the equivalence problem.
